items.explanation: The author argues that prediction matters most when it is risky and specific to one theory, and that fields differ in what kind of prediction they can support. The Ptolemaic example shows prediction alone does not prove truth, and the economics example shows precision standards cannot be uniform.
options: Prediction is the only valid test of a scientific theory, and theories that fail to predict should be discarded.
The Ptolemaic system proves that accurate prediction is evidence that a theory is true.
Prediction is a valuable but narrow test: it counts most when it is risky and specific to one theory, and different fields can support different kinds of prediction.
Economics and astronomy should be judged by the same standard of predictive precision.
items.passage: Prediction is the most prized achievement of science, and also its most misunderstood one. When a theory predicts an eclipse to the minute, or a particle that no instrument has yet seen, the success feels like proof that the theory has touched reality itself. Yet the history of science is full of theories that predicted brilliantly and were wrong. The Ptolemaic system predicted the positions of the planets with impressive accuracy for more than a thousand years, using a machinery of circles within circles that had no counterpart in the heavens. Its predictions worked because the mathematics was flexible enough to absorb each new observation, not because the earth stood at the centre of the universe. The lesson is not that prediction is worthless but that it is a narrower test than it appears. A theory earns credit when it predicts something its rivals cannot, and when the prediction is risky, when it could easily have failed. A prediction that any plausible theory would make tells us little. What matters is the prediction that only this theory, with its particular claims about the world, could have produced. This is why scientists distrust theories that can be stretched to fit any outcome. A theory that explains everything explains nothing, because it has given up the power to be surprised. The demand for risky prediction is a demand that a theory put its neck out. Where prediction becomes genuinely difficult is in systems with many interacting parts. No one expects a theory of economics to predict the price of wheat in ten years with the precision of an eclipse, and no one should. In such systems, small errors in measurement grow into large errors in outcome, and the system itself changes in response to being predicted. A forecast of a housing crash, if believed, changes the behaviour of buyers and sellers, and so changes the outcome it claimed to foresee. The failure of a prediction in these domains is therefore not always a failure of the theory. It may be a sign that the theory is about a world that refuses to sit still. The honest response is not to abandon prediction but to ask what kind of prediction a field can support. Astronomy can support precise point predictions. Economics can support predictions about tendencies, about what happens on average when a variable moves. Confusing the two is the error of both the sceptic who dismisses a science because it cannot forecast, and the enthusiast who claims more for a model than the subject allows. The history of medicine offers a useful parallel. A treatment that appears to work because patients recover may be doing nothing at all, since most patients recover without treatment. Only a controlled comparison, in which some patients receive the treatment and others do not, can show whether the treatment itself made the difference. Prediction in science works the same way: the test is not whether the outcome matches, but whether the match could have happened without the theory. A science is judged, in the end, not by whether it predicts everything, but by whether its predictions, where it makes them, are the kind that could have gone wrong.

items.explanation: The Ptolemaic system predicted planetary positions accurately for a thousand years, yet its circles had no counterpart in the heavens: the mathematics absorbed each observation. The lesson is that prediction is a narrower test than it appears, not that it is the only test, not that the system predicted badly, and not that prediction is worthless, since the passage explicitly says the lesson is not that prediction is worthless.
options: accurate prediction alone does not prove a theory true, because a flexible mathematics can absorb new observations without touching reality.
a theory that predicts well must be retained, since predictive success is the only test a theory can pass.
the Ptolemaic system failed because its predictions were inaccurate, and accuracy is what separates true theories from false ones.
prediction is worthless as a test, since even brilliant predictions can belong to false theories.

That is dismissal, not admiration, indifference or hope: flexibility here is a fault, not a strength, and the passage offers no repair for it.
options: dismissive, because such a theory has given up the power to be surprised.
admiring, because flexibility in the face of new evidence is a strength.
indifferent, because the passage treats stretchable theories as harmless.
hopeful, because such theories can always be repaired by adding new circles.

The failure of a prediction in such a system is therefore not always a failure of the theory. The example does not prove all forecasts wrong, does not claim crashes are unpredictable in principle, and the passage explicitly rejects judging economics by astronomy's standard.
options: To show that in systems that react to being predicted, a failed forecast need not mean the theory failed.
To prove that economic forecasts are always wrong and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: The passage says a service paid for directly by its users would have an incentive to respect their time, because wasted time would be a reason to cancel, while the present arrangement rewards the opposite: the more time a user wastes, the more the service earns. The first option states that contrast exactly.
options: A directly-paid service profits by respecting users' time, while an attention-funded service profits the more time users waste.
A directly-paid service profits by provoking outrage, while an attention-funded service profits by keeping users calm.
Both kinds of service profit in the same way, by charging users for the time they spend.
An attention-funded service profits by selling data, while a directly-paid service profits by selling attention.
items.passage: Nothing is free, and the things that claim to be free are often the most expensive. A search engine, a social network, a messaging service: each arrives without a price tag, and each is paid for in a currency its users rarely notice. The user is not the customer. The customer is the advertiser, and what the advertiser buys is the user's attention, measured, sorted and sold in parcels of seconds. This arrangement is usually described as a bargain. The user receives a service worth building, and in return surrenders a little data and a little time. The bargain looks fair only if the price is small and the user knows what it is. Neither condition holds. The data collected is not a little: it is a continuous record of location, contacts, habits and hesitations, detailed enough to predict behaviour the user has not yet decided on. And the user does not know the price, because the price is not stated anywhere. It is discovered later, in the form of a loan refused, an insurance premium raised, or a political advertisement aimed at a fear the user did not know had been recorded. Defenders of the arrangement reply that users consent, and that anyone who dislikes the terms can simply leave. Both claims are weaker than they look. Consent to a forty-page agreement written in legal language is not the same as understanding what is being given away, and leaving is not a real option when the service has become the way a person works, communicates and keeps in touch with family. A market in which the only alternative to accepting the terms is isolation is not a market that can be trusted to price anything fairly. The deeper problem is that the incentives of the seller and the user point in opposite directions. A service paid for by attention must maximise attention, and the surest way to maximise attention is to provoke emotion, preferably outrage, which holds the gaze longer than calm. A service paid for directly by its users would have an incentive to respect their time, because wasted time would be a reason to cancel. The present arrangement rewards the opposite: the more time a user wastes, the more the service earns. None of this means free services should disappear. They have brought genuine benefits, and a world in which only the wealthy could search, message and learn would be worse. The question is whether the price can be made visible and the incentives rebalanced, so that a user can know what a service costs and a service can profit without keeping its users agitated. Regulators have begun to notice. Several countries now require services to state plainly what data they collect and to obtain genuine consent, and some have fined companies that buried the terms in unreadable agreements. These measures help, but they do not change the underlying arithmetic: a service that earns money from attention will always be tempted to take more of it. Until then, the word free describes only the absence of a bill, not the absence of a cost.
items.question: The author argues that a service paid for by attention 'rewards the opposite' of what a directly-paid service rewards. Which of the following best captures the contrast?

items.explanation: The price is not stated anywhere; it is discovered later, in the form of a loan refused, an insurance premium raised, or a political advertisement aimed at a fear the user did not know had been recorded. The passage does not call the services a fraud, since they brought genuine benefits, does not blame the user, and explicitly says the data collected is not a little.
options: the price of a free service is discovered later, in concrete harms the user never agreed to pay.
free services are a fraud, since no service can ever be given away without a price.
users who are refused loans have only themselves to blame for surrendering their data.
the price of a free service is small, since it is paid in data rather than money.

The first option applies that mechanism to a new case. The others overstate it: automatically and never are too strong, and the passage says regulation helps but does not change the underlying arithmetic.
options: A new messaging app that charged a small monthly fee and carried no advertising would, on the author's reasoning, be less tempted to keep its users agitated than a free rival.
Any service that charges its users directly will automatically respect their time, whatever its design.

items.explanation: The author argues the loss that mattered was of ordinary records, birth registers, deeds and court files, and that without them disputes are settled by power, favouring the strong. Digital records face the same threat silently.
options: Famous historical documents matter more than ordinary records.
War is the only serious threat to archives.
The destruction of records harms ordinary people most, because records make everyday life legible and their loss hands power to the strong.
Digital records are indestructible and have solved the problem of preservation.
items.passage: In 1945, as the war in Europe ended, soldiers and archivists entering a ruined city found something stranger than the destruction of buildings: the destruction of records. Birth registers, land deeds, court files and parish books had burned, and with them the evidence that ordinary people had lived, owned, married and died in particular places. A family that could not prove it owned its house could lose it. A person who could not prove their age could not claim a pension. The loss was not of famous documents but of the paper that made everyday life legible to the law. Historians sometimes treat archives as the raw material of their craft, a convenience for research. That understates their role. An archive is the memory of a community that outlasts individual memory, and its destruction is a kind of amnesia imposed on people who never chose it. When records vanish, the past does not become mysterious in a romantic sense; it becomes contested. Two neighbours can remember the same boundary differently, and without a deed there is no way to settle the dispute except by power. The strongest party wins, which is another way of saying that the destruction of records transfers wealth and rights from the weak to the strong. Modern archives face a quieter version of the same threat. Paper rots slowly and visibly; digital records vanish suddenly and silently when a format becomes unreadable or a company closes. A photograph stored on a disc that no machine can read is as lost as a photograph burned in a fire, except that no one notices the loss until it is needed. The same logic applies to the records of ordinary institutions. A hospital that loses its patient files cannot prove what treatment was given; a school that loses its registers cannot prove who attended. The damage is rarely dramatic enough to make the news, which is precisely why it accumulates unnoticed. Each small loss seems tolerable on its own, and only when a dispute arises does the community discover how much it depended on paper it no longer has. The lesson of the ruined city is therefore not only about war. It is that a society which does not deliberately preserve its records will discover, too late, that it cannot prove what it once knew about itself.
items.question: Which of the following best captures the author's central argument?

items.explanation: The closing argument is that a society which does not deliberately preserve its records will discover too late that it cannot prove what it once knew. The first option narrows the harm to historians, but the passage says that understates the archive's role: the loss falls on ordinary people. The second contradicts the passage's claim that an archive is the memory of a community that outlasts individual memory. The third reverses the passage, which says the loss was not of famous documents but of the paper that made everyday life legible.
options: The destruction of records harms historians most, since archives are their raw material for research.
A community can reconstruct its past from living memory once its records are gone.
Record destruction matters only when famous documents are lost, since ordinary records are easily replaced.
A society that neglects preservation will eventually be unable to prove basic facts about itself.

items.explanation: The claim rests on a mechanism: without a deed there is no way to settle a dispute except by power, so the strongest party wins. If the losers were mostly the wealthy and the poor never held deeds, the loss would not transfer wealth from the weak to the strong, and the mechanism fails. The second and third options support the passage, and the fourth is only a partial exception: some families recovering does not change who generally loses.
options: In the ruined city, the families who lost their records were mostly wealthy landowners, while the poor had never held formal deeds at all.
Archives in other cities were also destroyed, and historians there found the loss equally damaging to research.
Digital records vanish more suddenly than paper records, and the loss is noticed only when the records are needed.
Some families in the ruined city kept copies of their deeds in other towns, and recovered their property without difficulty.
items.question: Which of the following statements, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the destruction of records transfers wealth and rights from the weak to the strong?

items.explanation: An archive is the memory of a community that outlasts individual memory, and its destruction is imposed amnesia: the past becomes contested, and the strongest party wins. The phrase is a metaphor for a community's loss, not a medical claim; the people never chose it, so the third option inverts it; and the passage stresses that the loss falls on ordinary people, not only on historians.
options: the loss of memory is inflicted on a community by destruction it did not choose, rather than a natural forgetting.
archives are literally the memory of individuals, and their destruction causes medical amnesia.
the people of the ruined city chose to forget their past, and the archive's destruction merely followed.
the destruction of records affects only historians, who lose their raw material.
items.question: The phrase 'a kind of amnesia imposed on people who never chose it' implies that:

items.explanation: The author argues creativity lives in choice, in deciding what to make, keep and discard, and that cheap making shifts the artist's job from producing to judging, so the machine is a more powerful brush, not the end of art. Only the last option holds both halves together. The first states the critic's postcard reply, that choosing is taste not making, as if it were the author's view, but the passage answers that reply rather than endorsing it. The second keeps the choice thesis but draws the opposite conclusion, that artists become unnecessary, while the passage says the machine moves the artist's work somewhere new. The third adds a condition the passage rejects: the photographer does not make the landscape and the collagist does not paint the fragments, yet both are called artists, so fabrication by hand is not required.
options: Creativity lies in the hand, and choosing among machine outputs is a matter of taste, not of making.
Creativity lies in choosing and judging, and the machine therefore makes human artists unnecessary.
Creativity lies in choosing and judging, but only when the artist also fabricates the material by hand.
Creativity lies in choosing and judging, so a machine is a tool that shifts the artist's work rather than ending it.
items.passage: When a machine produces a painting, who is the artist? The question sounds new, but it is an old one wearing new clothes. When photography arrived, painters complained that a machine had stolen their craft, and critics asked whether a photograph could be art at all. When synthesisers arrived, musicians were told that pressing a key was not playing. In each case the new tool was first dismissed as cheating, then absorbed, and finally used to make work that the old tools could not have made. The pattern suggests that the argument about machine art is less about the machine than about where we locate the creative act. If creativity lives in the hand, then a machine that moves the hand for you is a threat. If creativity lives in the choice, in deciding what to make, what to keep and what to discard, then a machine is only a more powerful brush. The person who generates a hundred images and hangs one has made a hundred decisions and kept one, and the keeping is the creative act. This does not settle the matter. A critic could reply that choosing among machine outputs is like choosing among postcards in a shop: a matter of taste, not of making. The reply has force, but it proves too much. Much of modern art already consists of choosing, arranging and framing things the artist did not fabricate. The photographer does not make the landscape, the collagist does not paint the fragments, and yet we call both artists. What matters, on this view, is not whether the hand touched the material but whether a guiding intelligence shaped the result. The honest conclusion is that the machine changes the economics of making, not the question of authorship. When making becomes cheap, choosing becomes the scarce skill, and the artist's job shifts from producing to judging. That shift is uncomfortable for those whose skill was in production, but discomfort is not an argument. The same pattern is visible in music, where the synthesiser was first condemned as a cheat and then became an instrument in its own right, and in writing, where the typewriter was once accused of destroying handwriting. In each case the tool changed what skill meant rather than abolishing skill. The photographers who survived were the ones who learned that the camera had not ended photography but had moved it somewhere new.
items.question: The author's central claim about machine-assisted art is that:

items.explanation: The author acknowledges the shift is uncomfortable for those whose skill was in production, but says discomfort is not an argument, and notes each new tool was first dismissed then absorbed. That is understanding without agreement.
options: sympathetic, because their skill in production is genuinely threatened.
contemptuous, because they understand nothing about art.
understanding of their discomfort but unconvinced by their argument.
indifferent, because the debate does not matter.
items.question: The author's attitude towards those who dismiss machine art as cheating can best be described as:

items.explanation: The person who generates a hundred images and hangs one has made a hundred decisions and kept one, and the keeping is the creative act, if creativity lives in the choice. The second option inverts the example, the third states the critic's reply, which the passage then answers rather than endorses, and the fourth overstates the parallel with photography, which the passage uses as an analogy, not an identity.
options: choosing among machine outputs can itself be the creative act, since the keeping is a decision.
generating many images proves the machine is the artist, since the person only presses a button.
the person who generates a hundred images has done no creative work at all, since the machine made them.
machine art is identical to photography, since both involve choosing among things the artist did not fabricate.
items.question: The example of the person who generates a hundred images and hangs one is meant to show that:

items.explanation: The closing sentence says the photographers who survived learned the camera had not ended photography but had moved it somewhere new, and the author presents this as the pattern for machine art generally. The first option states the fear the passage argues against. The third turns a first reaction into a permanent rule, but the passage says the new tool was first dismissed, then absorbed, then used to make work the old tools could not have made. The fourth invents a refusal the passage never describes.
options: The camera ended painting as an art form, and machine tools will end art altogether.
A new tool can move an art forward rather than ending it, when artists learn what the tool has changed.
Artists should resist new tools, because each one first arrives as cheating and is never absorbed.
Photography survived only because photographers refused to use the camera.

items.question: The sentences below, labelled A to D, form a coherent paragraph when arranged in the right order. Type the correct order as a four-letter sequence, for example ABCD. A: The new bus lane was painted overnight, and by morning the buses were moving twice as fast. B: Shopkeepers along the road said the lane had taken away their loading bays. items.question: The sentences below, labelled A to D, form a coherent paragraph when arranged in the right order. Type the correct order as a four-letter sequence, for example ABCD. A: The library's tool-lending scheme began with a simple observation: tools were bought, used once and thrown away. B: That growth has forced the library to track every loan, so it knows which tools are worth buying more of. C: The scheme has since grown to lend ladders, tents and sewing machines as well. D: That tracking is what lets a resident who needs a drill for a weekend borrow one instead of buying it.

BADC puts the inquiry's hearings before the inquiry is announced, BCAD puts the leak before the finding reaches the press, and CABD opens with the leak, which has no antecedent.

BADC

B: A team of engineers spent two years inspecting the dam's foundations. C: The leak forced the minister to order an inquiry into the very agency the report had criticised. D: The inquiry, once announced, could not be quietly closed, and its hearings exposed far more than the original report had.

items.explanation: The passage's point is the licence limit and its consequence: a bought book becomes a subscription. The first option invents a reader preference the passage never mentions, the third exaggerates the limit into a total refusal to sell, and the fourth denies the limit altogether. Only the second keeps both the mechanism, the expiring licence, and its consequence.
options: E-book lending has failed because readers prefer printed books to digital ones.
E-book licences, which expire after a fixed number of loans, turn the library's permanent collection into a subscription, even for books no one is reading.
Publishers have stopped selling books to libraries, so libraries can no longer lend anything at all.
Libraries lend e-books exactly as they lend printed books, with no limits of any kind.
items.question: Choose the best summary of this paragraph. Public libraries have begun lending e-books, and the change has exposed a problem no one planned for: a library can lend a printed book to one reader at a time, but an e-book licence often allows only a fixed number of loans before it expires, so a popular title can be unavailable even when no one is reading it. The limit is set by the publisher, not the library, and it turns a library's oldest principle, that a book once bought can be lent for ever, into a subscription.

items.explanation: The passage's argument is that individual cooling is not city cooling: the effect needs scale and must include the edge. The first option turns a qualification into a rejection, the third turns a warning about ignoring the edge into an instruction to ignore the centre, and the fourth claims warehouses are the whole cause, which the passage never says. Only the second keeps the claim, the scale condition and the edge.
options: White roofs are useless, and cities should stop painting them at once.
Painting roofs white cools individual buildings, but a city cools only if enough roofs change together, including the hard-to-paint warehouses on its edge.
Cities should paint only the roofs of warehouses and factories, and leave houses unpainted.
The heat of a city comes entirely from its warehouses, and houses play no part in it.
items.question: Choose the best summary of this paragraph. A city that paints its roofs white usually claims it is fighting heat, but the roofs that matter most are not the ones that are painted. A white roof cools the building beneath it, yet the city as a whole cools only when enough roofs change together, and the buildings whose roofs are hardest to paint, the warehouses and factories on the edge of town, are the ones that absorb the most heat. A programme that paints houses in the centre and ignores the edge will therefore cool the comfortable and leave the hot places hot.

items.explanation: Step 1, the causal gap: the conclusion is that free books caused the rise, but the evidence is only that the rise followed the change and that students reported a cost barrier, so the argument needs the rise to have no other cause. Step 2, the negation test: if the pilot college had also introduced easier exams or extra tutoring, the rise could be explained without the free books, so the first option is required and the argument fails without it. Step 3, necessary against merely supportive: the second option would strengthen the argument by tying use to the students who needed the books, but the argument could still hold if the books were used just as much by other students, so it is not required. The third option claims far more than the argument needs, since the argument needs only that the free books helped in this pilot, not that every passing student reads the book through, and the fourth option is about a preference that says nothing about pass rates. Only the first option is an assumption the argument relies on.
options: The pilot college introduced no other change, such as easier exams or extra tutoring, that could on its own explain the rise in pass rates.
The students who had been unable to afford the books used the free books more than other students did.
Every student who passes a course reads the set textbook from cover to cover.
Students prefer reading on a screen to reading a printed book.
items.question: A publisher argues that making its textbooks free online will increase the number of students who pass its courses. It points out that in a pilot college, pass rates rose after the textbooks were made free, and that students there said cost had stopped them buying the books before the pilot. The publisher's argument relies on which of the following assumptions?

items.explanation: The coherent paragraph is 1-2-3-4: the museum extends its hours, those hours are filled with lectures, the lectures prove popular enough to add a second session, and evening attendance doubles. Each sentence is tied to the next by a reference: those extra hours in 2 needs 1, the lectures in 3 needs 2, and the doubling in 4 is the result of the lectures. Sentence 5 is about the gift shop's hours and sales, a different subject with its own result, and it has no link to the lectures, the second session, or the attendance that doubles in 4. It shares the museum and the evening with the paragraph, which is what makes it tempting, but it belongs to no part of the lectures argument. No other sentence can be the odd one: dropping 1 leaves those extra hours in 2 without an antecedent, dropping 2 leaves the lectures in 3 without their introduction, and dropping 3 leaves the doubling in 4 without its cause.
items.question: Five jumbled up sentences, labelled 1 to 5, related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer. 1: The museum extended its opening hours to attract evening visitors. 2: Those extra hours were filled with evening lectures, which gave visitors a reason to return after dark. 3: The lectures proved so popular that the museum added a second evening session each week. 4: Within a year, evening attendance had doubled, and the museum made the longer hours permanent. 5: The museum had also extended its gift shop hours that year, and the shop's evening sales had risen.

items.explanation: Firm C existed from 2018 to 2021 and raised 8 crore in total, with 1 crore in 2018 and 1 crore in 2021, so its 2019 and 2020 amounts add up to 6 crore. Each amount is at most 3 crore, because it can rise by at most 2 from the previous year and must fall back to 1 in the last year, so both middle years must be exactly 3 crore. C's 2019 amount is therefore 3 crore.

In any year, a firm's amount changed by at most Rs 2 crore from the previous year. All amounts are whole numbers of crores. The table gives each firm's first year, last year and total amount raised.
items.question: What is the amount raised by firm C in 2019, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Take the largest possible 2020 amount for each firm and add them. A can reach 4, B can reach 3, C is fixed at 3, D is in its first year at 1, and E can reach 3, giving a largest possible total of 14 crore. The firms are independent, so the maxima can all happen together.
items.question: What is the largest possible total amount raised by all five firms in 2020, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Take the smallest possible 2021 amount for each firm and add them. A cannot go below 3, B cannot go below 1, C is in its last year at 1, D cannot go below 2 and E cannot go below 2, giving a smallest possible total of 9 crore. Each minimum is reachable on its own, and the firms are independent.
items.question: What is the smallest possible total amount raised by all five firms in 2021, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Firm A is forced to 1, 3, 4, 3, 1 and firm C to 1, 3, 3, 1, so in 2021 firm A raised 3 crore and firm C raised 1 crore, and firms B, D and E together raised 14 minus 4, which is 10 crore. Each of B, D and E has a largest possible 2021 amount. For B, the middle three years sum to 7, and if 2021 were 4 or more, both neighbours would be at least 2, since each changes by at most 2 from 2021, so the three years would sum to at least 8, above 7; so B raised at most 3 in 2021. For D, the 2021 and 2022 amounts sum to 5 and each is at most 3, since 2021 follows the first year amount of 1 and 2022 must fall back to 1 in 2023, so D raised at most 3 in 2021. For E, the middle three years sum to 8, and if 2021 were 5, both neighbours would be at least 3, so the three years would sum to at least 11, above 8; so E raised at most 4 in 2021, and 4 is reachable, in 1, 2, 4, 2, 1. So B, D and E together raised at most 3 plus 3 plus 4, which is 10 crore, and they did raise 10 crore, so each firm must be at its maximum: B raised 3, D raised 3 and E raised 4 in 2021. The first option is therefore true. The second option fails because D raised 3, not 2; the third fails because E raised 4, not 3; the fourth fails because B raised 3, not 2. The trap is capping E at 3, which makes the total of 14 look impossible.
options: Firm B raised Rs 3 crore in 2021.
Firm D raised Rs 2 crore in 2021.
Firm E raised Rs 3 crore in 2021.
Firm B raised Rs 2 crore in 2021.
items.question: Suppose it is now revealed that the five firms together raised exactly Rs 14 crore in 2021. Which of the following statements must be true?

items.explanation: Firm A existed from 2018 to 2022 and raised 12 crore in total, so its 2019, 2020 and 2021 amounts add up to 10 crore. Its 2020 amount is at most 4 crore, reached when the sequence is 1, 3, 4, 3, 1, which respects the step limit of 2 crore per year and sums to 12. A larger 2020 amount would force the total above 12.
items.question: What is the largest possible amount raised by firm A in 2020, in Rs crore?

diagram.caption: Eight friends around a circular table, facing the centre
diagram.content: A sits opposite D. B sits two seats clockwise from A. E sits immediately clockwise from B. C sits immediately clockwise from D. F sits immediately anticlockwise from G. H sits between A and B.

items.explanation: Going clockwise the order is A, H, B, E, D, C, F, G. B is at the third seat clockwise from A, so the seat opposite B is four places away, which is F. H sits next to B, and G sits next to F, so neither can be opposite B.
options: G
C
H
F
items.question: Who sits opposite B?

items.explanation: Solving the clues gives the clockwise order A, H, B, E, D, C, F, G. Swapping H and B gives A, B, H, E, D, C, F, G, in which the seat clockwise from F is G. The swap changes the neighbours of H and B only, but the question cannot be answered without first solving the whole arrangement, and reading the original order instead of the swapped one gives H.
options: G
H
A
D
items.question: Eight friends sit around a circular table facing the centre, in the order given in the set. If H and B swap seats with each other, who sits immediately clockwise from F?

items.explanation: C is the sixth seat clockwise from A. Counting two seats anticlockwise from C gives the fourth seat clockwise from A, which is E. D is only one seat anticlockwise from C, and F is three seats away.
options: D
F
E
B
items.question: Who sits two seats anticlockwise from C?

items.explanation: The solved clockwise order is A, H, B, E, D, C, F, G. After E and C swap, the order is A, H, B, C, D, E, F, G. The seat opposite B is four places away, which is F. A solver who swaps the wrong pair, or who reads the opposite seat in the original order, gets D.
options: F
D
G
E
items.question: Eight friends sit around a circular table facing the centre, in the order given in the set. If E and C swap seats with each other, who sits opposite B?

items.explanation: Solving the clues gives the clockwise order A, H, B, E, D, C, F, G. Swapping H and B gives A, B, H, E, D, C, F, G. In the swapped order, going clockwise from B to G passes H, E, D, C and F, five people, while going the other way passes only A, one person. The shorter side therefore has 1 person between them. Reading the original order instead of the swapped one gives 2, and counting only one way round gives 5.
items.question: Eight friends sit around a circular table facing the centre, in the order given in the set. If H and B swap seats with each other, how many people sit between B and G, counting along the shorter side of the table?

diagram.caption: Six-team round robin after 4 rounds (win 2 points, draw 1)

items.explanation: After the final round the points are P 7, Q 7, R 6, T 5, S 3 and U 2. P and Q tie at the top on 7 points, so the next team, R on 6 points, finishes third.
options: Q
T
S
R
items.question: If P loses to T, Q draws with U and R beats S, which team finishes third?

items.explanation: Only three teams can finish on 5 points. P starts on 7 and can only stay or rise, Q starts on 6 and can only stay or rise, and U starts on 1 and can reach at most 3. R reaches 5 only by drawing with S, S reaches 5 only by beating R, and T reaches 5 only by beating P. But R and S play each other, so they cannot both finish on 5: a draw puts R on 5 and S on 4, while an S win puts S on 5 and R on 4. Since exactly two teams finish on 5 and at most one of R and S can be among them, T must be the other one, so T beat P. The second team on 5 is R if the R-S match is drawn and S if S wins, so neither of those results is forced, and the Q-U result is not constrained by the count at all.
options: P lost to T
R drew with S
S beat R
Q drew with U
items.question: In the final round, P plays T, Q plays U and R plays S. After the final round, exactly two teams finish on 5 points. Which of the following must have happened in the final round?

items.explanation: S beats R, so S finishes on 3 + 2 = 5 points and R stays on 4. P draws with T, so P finishes on 7 + 1 = 8 points and T on 3 + 1 = 4. Q already has 6 points, so whatever happens against U, Q finishes on at least 6. The final order is therefore P on 8, Q on at least 6, and S on 5, so S can finish no higher than third. The second option is the highest position S can reach, and no result in the Q-U match can lift S above third, since Q cannot fall below 6 points.
options: Second
Third
Fourth
Fifth
items.question: If S beats R and T draws with P, what is the highest position S can finish in?

items.explanation: P already has 7 points and Q already has 6, so two teams are certain. R has 4 points and one match left, so R can reach 6 by beating S. S, T and U can reach at most 5, 5 and 3, so they cannot reach 6. The maximum is therefore 3 teams: P, Q and R.
items.question: What is the maximum number of teams that can finish on 6 or more points?

items.explanation: Q beats U, so Q finishes on 6 + 2 = 8 points. P loses to T, so P stays on 7 points and T rises to 3 + 2 = 5. R and S play each other, so at most one of them can reach 6 points, and neither can pass 7. The final order is therefore Q on 8, P on 7, and no other team above 6, so the second-placed team finishes with 7 points.
items.question: If Q beats U and P loses to T, how many points does the second-placed team finish with?

diagram.caption: Five friends, each with a favourite colour, sport and pet
diagram.content: Each friend has a different favourite colour, a different sport and a different pet. Each of the five listed categories in each group is assigned to exactly one friend. Amit likes Red and does not play Cricket. Bina plays Tennis and has a Cat. Chetan does not like Green and does not have a Bird. Chetan does not like Yellow. Amit does not have a Fish. Divya has a Bird and does not like White. Esha likes Green. The person who plays Cricket likes Blue. The person who likes Yellow plays Football. The person who has a Fish plays Badminton. The person who plays Hockey has a Rabbit. The person who likes White plays Tennis.

items.explanation: Solving the whole grid gives Esha Green, and the only pet left for the Green holder once the other four pets are placed is Fish. The answer is not stated anywhere in the clues; it follows only from completing the assignment, since Esha's pet is fixed by elimination. The set material states the one-to-one rule, so each colour, sport and pet belongs to exactly one friend.
options: Dog
Cat
Bird
Fish
items.question: Which pet does Esha have?

items.explanation: The set states that each friend has a different colour, sport and pet. Divya has a Bird, so she cannot play Hockey (whose player has a Rabbit) or Badminton (whose player has a Fish). She does not like White, and the Tennis player likes White, so she does not play Tennis. For colours, Amit likes Red, Esha likes Green and Bina, who plays Tennis, likes White; Chetan does not like Yellow, so Chetan likes Blue and Divya likes Yellow. The person who likes Yellow plays Football, so Divya plays Football.
options: Football
Cricket
Tennis
Badminton
items.question: Which sport does Divya play?

items.explanation: The solved assignment is: Amit likes Red, plays Hockey and has a Rabbit; Bina likes White, plays Tennis and has a Cat; Chetan likes Blue, plays Cricket and has a Dog; Divya likes Yellow, plays Football and has a Bird; Esha likes Green, plays Badminton and has a Fish. Only the statement about Amit holds in this assignment; each of the other three contradicts it, and none of them can be checked without solving the whole grid.
options: Amit plays Hockey
Chetan has a Rabbit
Divya likes Blue
Bina has a Fish
items.question: Which of the following statements about the five friends must be true?

items.explanation: The set material now states the one-to-one rule, so each colour, sport and pet belongs to exactly one friend. The person who plays Hockey has a Rabbit. Working through the clues, the Hockey player is Amit, and Amit likes Red, so the Rabbit owner's colour is Red. The Cricket player likes Blue, which is Chetan, not the Rabbit owner.
options: Red
Blue
Green
Yellow
items.question: What colour does the person who has a Rabbit like?

items.explanation: With the clue removed, Bina is still fixed at White, Tennis and Cat, Divya still has a Bird and does not like White, and Esha still likes Green. The remaining clues then leave exactly five assignments. In the first, Amit likes Red, plays Hockey and has a Rabbit, Chetan likes Blue, plays Cricket and has a Dog, Divya likes Yellow and plays Football, and Esha plays Badminton and has a Fish. In the second and third, Amit likes Blue, plays Cricket and has a Dog, Divya likes Yellow and plays Football, Esha plays Hockey and has a Rabbit, and Chetan likes Red and either plays Badminton and has a Fish or plays Hockey and has a Rabbit, with Esha taking the other sport and pet. In the fourth and fifth, Amit likes Yellow, plays Football and has a Dog, Divya likes Blue, plays Cricket and has a Bird, Esha plays Hockey and has a Rabbit, and again Chetan likes Red and either plays Badminton and has a Fish or plays Hockey and has a Rabbit, with Esha taking the other sport and pet. No other assignment satisfies the remaining clues, so the count is 5.
items.question: The five friends are Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya and Esha. The five colours are Red, White, Blue, Yellow and Green. The five sports are Cricket, Tennis, Football, Badminton and Hockey. The five pets are Cat, Dog, Bird, Fish and Rabbit. If the clue that Amit likes Red and does not play Cricket were removed, how many different assignments of a colour, a sport and a pet to each of the five friends would satisfy all the remaining clues?

diagram.caption: Monthly production of two factories, Jan-Jun 2024 (thousand units)

items.explanation: The ratios of B to A are Jan: 90/120 = 75.0%, Feb: 110/140 = 78.6%, Mar: 130/130 = 100.0%, Apr: 120/160 = 75.0%, May: 130/150 = 86.7%, Jun: 140/180 = 77.8%. Only Mar reaches 90%, so the count is 1. Comparing absolute production instead of the ratio would count months where B is merely close in absolute terms.
items.question: In how many months was Factory B's production at least 90% of Factory A's production in the same month?

items.explanation: Factory A's production grew from 150 in May to 180 in June, a rise of 30 on 150, which is 20 percent. Applying the same 20 percent rise to Factory B's May figure of 130 gives 130 x 1.20 = 156 thousand units. The combined June production would then have been 180 + 156 = 336 thousand units.
items.question: If Factory B's production in June had instead grown from May by the same percentage as Factory A's production grew from May to June, what would the combined June production have been, in thousand units?

items.explanation: Let the apples be 5k and the mangoes 2k. The oranges are 44, so 110 + 44 + 44 = 198 gives k = 22. Unsold apples are 30, unsold mangoes 16 and unsold oranges half of 44, which is 22, and indeed 30 : 22 reduces to 15 : 11. The total unsold is 30 + 16 + 22 = 68. Counting the full oranges, or reporting the sold fruit instead, gives the wrong options.
items.question: A fruit vendor has 198 pieces of fruit in total: apples, mangoes and oranges. Apples and mangoes are in the ratio 5 : 2. She then sells 80 apples, 28 mangoes and half of the oranges, after which the apples still unsold and the oranges still unsold are in the ratio 15 : 11. How many pieces of fruit remain unsold in total?

items.explanation: The cost prices are 1800/1.2 = Rs 1,500, 2400/0.75 = Rs 3,200 and 3000/1.25 = Rs 2,400, giving a total cost of Rs 7,100 against total selling price Rs 7,200, so the overall result is a profit of Rs 100.
options: Loss of Rs 100
Profit of Rs 200
No profit, no loss
Profit of Rs 100
items.question: A trader sells three articles for Rs 1,800, Rs 2,400 and Rs 3,000. On the first he gains 20%, on the second he loses 25%, and on the third he gains 25%. What is his overall profit or loss, in rupees?
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Single formula applied twice: derive each cost price from its selling price and percentage, then compare totals. School-level profit and loss.

items.explanation: Let the roots be 3t and 4t. Their product is 12 t^2 = 108, so t^2 = 9 and t = 3, giving roots 9 and 12. Then a^2 + b^2 = 81 + 144 = 225. The sum of the roots is 21, but squaring the sum alone counts 2ab twice, which is the trap in the largest distractor.
items.question: The roots of x^2 - Sx + 108 = 0 are positive integers in the ratio 3 : 4. What is the value of a^2 + b^2, where a and b are the roots?

items.explanation: For two years the difference between compound and simple interest is P x (r/100)^2, so P x (8/100)^2 = 72 gives P = Rs 11,250. The simple interest on Rs 11,250 at 12% for 3 years is 11250 x 12 x 3 / 100 = Rs 4,050.
items.question: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum at 8% per annum for 2 years is Rs 72. The same sum is then lent at 12% per annum simple interest for 3 years. What is the simple interest earned in the second lending, in rupees?
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: One interest formula family: derive the principal from the CI-SI difference, then apply simple interest. Two applications of the same concept.

items.explanation: Since log_4(x^2) = log_2(x^2) / log_2(4) = log_2 x, the condition is 2 log_2 x <= 20, so log_2 x <= 10 and x <= 1024. The largest perfect square not exceeding 1024 is 32^2 = 1024. A solver who converts only one logarithm, or who forgets the perfect-square condition and answers 1024, misses the final step.
items.question: What is the largest perfect square x such that log_2(x) + log_4(x^2) does not exceed 20?

items.explanation: The hypotenuse is sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = 15 cm, so AP + PB = 15. The condition CP^2 = AP x PB gives AP x PB = 36, so AP and PB are the two roots of u^2 - 15u + 36 = 0, which are 12 and 3. Since AP is the larger, AP = 12 cm. Using CP as if it were the altitude, or taking the smaller root, gives the wrong options.
items.question: In triangle ABC, angle C is a right angle, AC = 9 cm and BC = 12 cm. A point P lies on the hypotenuse AB such that CP = 6 cm and CP^2 = AP x PB. If AP is greater than PB, what is the length of AP, in cm?

items.explanation: Meeting after 1 hour 30 minutes over 45 km gives Amit's speed plus Rohan's speed = 30 km/h. The time difference gives 45/v_Amit - 45/v_Rohan = 1 hour 15 minutes. Solving the two equations together gives Amit's speed 12 km/h and Rohan's 18 km/h. The meeting equation alone cannot fix either speed, and swapping who is slower gives 18 km/h, the trap option.
items.question: Towns A and B are 45 km apart, joined by a straight road. Amit travels from A to B while Rohan travels from B to A. They set off at the same time and pass each other after 1 hour 30 minutes. Amit gets to B 1 hour 15 minutes after Rohan gets to A. What is Amit's speed, in km per hour?

items.explanation: If the roots are integers a and b with a not equal to b, then a + b = 13 and k = ab. The possible pairs (a, b) with a < b are (1, 12), (2, 11), (3, 10), (4, 9), (5, 8), (6, 7), giving the distinct products 12, 22, 30, 36, 40, 42, so there are 6 possible values of k. Counting ordered pairs would double the answer, and allowing a = b would add one more value, both of which are the traps.
items.question: For how many integer values of k does the equation x^2 - 13x + k = 0 have two distinct integer roots?

items.explanation: Since 7 squared is 49, which leaves remainder 24 on division by 25, that is, 49 is congruent to -1 modulo 25. Then 7^10 is (7^2)^5, which is congruent to (-1)^5, that is -1, which is 24 modulo 25. Working with 7^10 modulo 5 instead gives 4, which answers a different question.
items.question: What is the remainder when 7^10 is divided by 25?

items.explanation: After each operation the milk is multiplied by 80/100 = 4/5. After one operation there are 80 litres, after two 64 litres, and continuing gives 4096/125 litres after 5 operations, which is the first value below 40 litres. Treating the draw as a fixed subtraction of 20 litres each time would give a much smaller count.
items.question: A vessel holds 100 litres of milk. Each time, 20 litres are drawn out and replaced with water, so the milk is diluted. After how many such operations will the amount of milk left in the vessel first fall below 40 litres?

items.explanation: Let the radii be R and r with R + r = 13 and R - r = 5, so R = 9 and r = 4. For a direct common tangent, the length AB satisfies AB squared = d squared - (R - r) squared = 169 - 25 = 144, so AB = 12 cm.
items.question: Two circles touch each other externally. The distance between their centres is 13 cm and the difference between their radii is 5 cm. A direct common tangent touches the circles at A and B. What is the length of AB, in cm?

items.explanation: A and B together do 3 x (1/12 + 1/18) = 5/12 of the work in 3 days, leaving 7/12. The three together finish that in 3 days, so their combined rate is 7/36 per day, and C's rate is 7/36 - 5/36 = 1/18 per day, so C alone would take 18 days. C works for 3 days at 1/18 per day, doing 1/6 of the work.
options: 18 days / 1/4
24 days / 1/6
18 days / 1/6
12 days / 1/6
items.question: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 3 days, then C joins them and the three finish the remaining work in 3 days. How many days would C take to do the work alone, and what fraction of the whole work did C do? Give the days first, then the fraction.
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Single work-rate formula: joint work for 4 days, remainder over B's rate. One concept, mechanical.

items.explanation: The sum is 10/2 x (10 + 9 x d) = 50 + 45 x d, where d is the common difference. Requiring 230 <= sum <= 410 leaves the sums 230, 275, 320, 365, 410, which is 5 distinct values. Counting every integer in the interval, instead of only those the sum formula can produce, overcounts the answer.
items.question: An arithmetic progression has 10 terms and first term 5. Its common difference is a positive integer and the sum of all its terms lies between 230 and 410 inclusive. How many distinct values can the sum of the progression take?

items.explanation: Of the 1000 people, 100 have the condition and 900 do not. After the first test there are 90 true positives and 45 false positives. The second test keeps 72 of the true positives and 9/2 of the false positives, so among double positives the share who really have the condition is 72 / (72 + 9/2) = 16/17. Stopping after the first test, or quoting the second test's sensitivity alone, gives the wrong options.
items.question: In a population of 1000 people, 10% have a certain condition. A first test detects the condition in 90% of those who have it and wrongly reports it in 5% of those who do not. Everyone who tests positive on the first test takes a second, independent test, which detects the condition in 80% of those who have it and wrongly reports it in 10% of those who do not. What is the probability that a person who tests positive on both tests actually has the condition?

items.explanation: The scores total 30 x 40 = 1200. To push the lowest score as high as possible, the other 29 scores must be packed at the top of the range. With lowest score 25 a set of distinct scores totalling 1200 exists, while a lowest score of 26 forces even the smallest possible total above 1200, which is impossible. Hence the greatest possible lowest score is 25.
items.question: A class has 30 students whose scores are all distinct integers between 0 and 100 inclusive, and the class average is 40. What is the greatest possible score of the lowest-scoring student?

items.explanation: The powers of 3 modulo 7 run 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 and then repeat, so 3^n leaves remainder 1 exactly when n is a multiple of 6, not when n is 5 more than a multiple of 6. The multiples of 6 up to 200 are 6, 12, ..., 198, which is 33 numbers. Their sum is 6 times (1 + 2 + ... + 33), and 1 + 2 + ... + 33 is 33 x 34 / 2 = 561, so the sum is 6 x 561 = 3366. Counting the values instead of summing them, or using the wrong residue class, gives a different answer.
items.question: What is the sum of all integers n with 1 <= n <= 200 such that 3^n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 7?

items.explanation: The first inequality holds exactly for 3 < x < 11, which is 7 integers. The second requires |x| < sqrt(100), so x lies between -10 and 10. Intersecting the two ranges leaves 6 integers. Counting the first range alone, or forgetting that the second range cuts off the top end, gives the wrong options.
items.question: How many integers x satisfy both (x - 3)(x - 11) < 0 and x^2 < 100?

items.explanation: Let the quantities be 4k and 3k. After the first move they are 4k - 10 and 3k + 10, and the ratio 3 : 4 gives k = 10, so the quantities are 40 and 30, and after the move 30 and 40. Moving 5 units back gives 35 and 35, a ratio of 1 : 1. The second move does not simply undo the first, since only 5 units move back, so the original ratio of 4 : 3 is not restored.
items.question: Two quantities are in the ratio 4 : 3. If 10 units are moved from the first quantity to the second, the ratio becomes 3 : 4. If 5 more units are then moved from the second quantity back to the first, what is the ratio of the first quantity to the second?

items.explanation: Let the edges be m - d, m and m + d. Their sum is 3m = 30, so m = 10. The surface area is 2(lm + mn + nl) = 582, so l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 30^2 - 582 = 318. But l^2 + m^2 + n^2 is also 3m^2 + 2d^2 = 300 + 2d^2, giving d^2 = 9 and d = 3. The longest edge is m + d = 13 cm. The middle edge alone, or the sum of squares itself, would answer a different question.
items.question: A cuboid has edges in arithmetic progression. The sum of its three edges is 30 cm and its total surface area is 582 sq cm. What is the length of its longest edge, in cm?

items.explanation: Treat the 3 girls as a single block. Then there are 6 units (5 boys plus the block) to arrange in 6! = 720 ways, and the girls can be arranged within their block in 3! = 6 ways. The total is 720 into 6 = 4320. The block method is the standard way to handle togetherness conditions.
items.question: In how many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls be seated in a row so that all 3 girls sit together?

items.explanation: Set y = 3^x. Then y^2 - y - 72 = 0, which factors as (y - 9)(y + 8) = 0. Since 3^x is positive, y = 9, so 3^x = 9 and x = 2. The negative root y = -8 is rejected because an exponential can never be negative.
items.question: If 3^(2x) - 3^x = 72, what is x?

items.explanation: There are 27 outcomes in which the product is even, out of 36 in total. Of those, 3 have a sum greater than 10: (5, 6), (6, 5) and (6, 6). Only the first two have different numbers, so the conditional probability is 2/27. Counting (6, 6) as well gives 1/9, and dividing by 36 instead of by the 27 outcomes in the condition gives the other wrong options.
items.question: Two fair dice are thrown. Given that the product of the two numbers shown is even, what is the probability that their sum is greater than 10 and the two numbers are different?
